title: Replication, transcription, translation and mutation
blurb: Follow genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein, decode codons, and predict how each type of mutation changes the protein.
question: In sickle cell anemia, one DNA base change makes hemoglobin fold into the wrong shape. How does a change in DNA reach the protein, and why can one wrong base matter so much while some other base changes do nothing at all?

teach.body: Formal statement: genetic information flows DNA to RNA to protein. DNA is copied by replication; transcription makes an RNA copy of a gene; translation reads the RNA to build a protein. Plain English: the DNA master recipe never leaves the kitchen office (the nucleus). The cell writes a working copy (mRNA), carries it to the kitchen counter (the ribosome) and cooks the dish (the protein) by following it, three letters at a time.

teach.caption: Replication happens in S phase, in the nucleus. It is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one old strand and gains one new strand. The leading strand is made continuously, the lagging strand in pieces.

teach.body: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand and builds complementary mRNA: DNA A gives mRNA U, T gives A, G gives C, and C gives G. In eukaryotes the first transcript (pre-mRNA) is processed before it leaves the nucleus: introns (intervening sequences) are removed, exons (expressed sequences) are spliced together, and a 5' cap and poly-A tail are added. The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA, with T in place of U.

teach.caption: The code is redundant (degenerate), unambiguous (each codon means one thing) and nearly universal across organisms.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Devon decodes one codon
teach.body: Devon, a nursing applicant, follows one codon. The DNA template strand reads 3'-TAC-5'. Transcription pairs T with A, A with U and C with G, giving mRNA 5'-AUG-3'. At the ribosome, a tRNA with the anticodon UAC pairs with AUG and delivers methionine, the start amino acid. The coding strand would read 5'-ATG-3': the mRNA sequence with T instead of U.

teach.caption: Deleting exactly 3 bases removes one amino acid without a frameshift. Causes: replication errors and mutagens (UV, X-rays, some chemicals, tobacco smoke). Only mutations in gametes are inherited.
In sickle cell anemia, valine replaces glutamic acid in beta-globin; the changed primary structure alters the shape, and the shape alters the function.

teach.text: Watch for reversals: transcription is in the NUCLEUS, translation at RIBOSOMES; mRNA carries CODONS, tRNA carries the ANTICODON; AUG is START, not stop; introns are removed and exons kept; replication is SEMIconservative; and a silent mutation does not change the protein.

items: Replication (S phase): helicase unzips, DNA polymerase builds 5' to 3', ligase joins Okazaki fragments; semiconservative.
Transcription (nucleus): RNA polymerase makes mRNA; introns out, exons spliced.
Translation (ribosome): codons read by tRNA anticodons; peptide bonds join amino acids.
64 codons, 20 amino acids; AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop.
Silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift; sequence sets shape, shape sets function.

summary: You can now describe semiconservative replication and its enzymes, convert a DNA template into mRNA and then into amino acids, and use the start and stop codons. You can also predict the effect of silent, missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations and link amino acid sequence to protein shape and function.

A.q: During DNA replication, which enzyme unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases?
A.why: Helicase unwinds and unzips the double helix, breaking the hydrogen bonds between paired bases.

whyNot.0: DNA ligase seals Okazaki fragments together on the lagging strand.
whyNot.1: DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides and proofreads; it needs the strands already separated.
whyNot.3: RNA polymerase transcribes DNA into mRNA; it does not run replication.

A.q: Where does translation take place in a eukaryotic cell?
options: In the nucleus on the DNA template
A.why: Translation happens at ribosomes in the cytoplasm (free or on rough ER), where mRNA codons are read.

whyNot.1: The nucleus is where transcription happens; translation follows in the cytoplasm.
whyNot.2: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and ribosome subunits; it does not translate mRNA.
whyNot.3: The Golgi modifies and packages finished proteins; it does not build them.

A.q: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because:
options: Both old strands stay together in one helix
Each strand is a random mix of old and new DNA
Half of the genes are copied in each S phase
Each new helix has one old and one new strand
A.why: Each original strand serves as a template, so every new double helix keeps one parental strand and one newly built strand.

whyNot.0: Keeping both old strands together would be conservative replication, which is not what happens.
whyNot.1: A patchwork of old and new segments within each strand does not describe DNA replication.
whyNot.2: The entire genome is copied once in S phase; "semi" refers to strands, not to half the genes.

B.q: An mRNA codon reads 5'-AUG-3'. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is a stop codon that ends translation
It is the start codon for methionine
Its tRNA anticodon is also AUG
It codes for three amino acids
B.why: AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine.

whyNot.0: The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA; AUG starts translation.
whyNot.2: The anticodon is complementary to the codon, so it reads UAC.
whyNot.3: Each codon of three bases codes for ONE amino acid.

B.q: Which mutation would most likely have the GREATEST effect on the protein a gene codes for?
options: Insertion of one base near the gene's start
Substitution that gives a synonymous codon
Deletion of three bases near the gene's end
Substitution of one base in the final codon
B.why: Inserting one base early shifts the reading frame, so nearly every amino acid after it changes: a frameshift.

whyNot.1: A synonymous codon codes for the same amino acid: a silent mutation with no effect.
whyNot.2: Deleting three bases removes one amino acid without shifting the frame, and near the end it affects little.
whyNot.3: A substitution in the last codon changes at most one amino acid at the end of the chain.

B.q: A DNA template strand reads 3'-TACGGA-5'. Which mRNA is transcribed from it?
B.why: Pair each template base: T to A, A to U, C to G, G to C, giving 5'-AUGCCU-3'.

whyNot.0: ATGCCT is the coding DNA strand; mRNA uses uracil, not thymine.
whyNot.1: This copies the template with U swapped in, instead of pairing each base.
whyNot.3: This simply repeats the template; mRNA must be complementary to it.

C.q: In sickle cell anemia, one base change replaces glutamic acid with valine in the beta-globin chain. This is an example of a:
C.why: A single base substitution that swaps one amino acid for another is a missense mutation.

whyNot.0: A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged; here glutamic acid becomes valine.
whyNot.1: A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon and shortens the protein.
whyNot.2: A frameshift comes from inserting or deleting bases, not from one substitution.

C.q: Which statement about the genetic code is correct?
options: One codon can specify several amino acids
Many amino acids have more than one codon
There are 64 amino acids and 20 codons
Each codon is a pair of two mRNA bases
C.why: The code is redundant: 61 codons cover 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.

whyNot.0: The code is unambiguous: each codon specifies just one amino acid (or stop).
whyNot.2: Reversed: there are 64 codons and 20 amino acids.
whyNot.3: A codon is three bases, not two.

C.q: A DNA template strand contains 3'-TAC-5'. Which tRNA anticodon pairs with the resulting mRNA codon, and which amino acid does it carry?
C.why: TAC transcribes to mRNA AUG; the complementary anticodon is UAC, and AUG codes for methionine.

whyNot.1: AUG is the mRNA codon; the anticodon is its complement, UAC.
whyNot.2: AUG is the start codon for methionine, not a stop signal.
whyNot.3: ATG is the coding DNA sequence; tRNA uses uracil and is complementary to the codon.

reteach.title: The recipe book in the office
reteach.question: A restaurant keeps its master recipe book locked in the office. How do the cooks make a dish without ever taking the book into the kitchen?

blocks.body: The master book is DNA, locked in the office (nucleus). Photocopying the whole book for a new branch is replication. Copying one recipe onto a card is transcription: the card is mRNA. Crossing out the chef's side notes (introns) and keeping the steps (exons) is processing. At the counter (ribosome), kitchen staff (tRNA) read the card three words at a time (codons) and fetch each ingredient (amino acid). A typo on the card can change one ingredient, or garble the whole recipe if it shifts every word.

blocks.text: A typo that swaps one word for a synonym changes nothing (silent); a missing letter that shifts every later word (frameshift) ruins the dish.

explain.body: In S phase: helicase unzips; primase adds an RNA primer; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides 5' to 3' and proofreads; the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase. Each new helix has one old and one new strand.

test.q: On the lagging strand, short Okazaki fragments are joined together by:
test.why: DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments to make a continuous strand.

whyNot.0: Helicase unwinds the helix at the start of replication.
whyNot.2: Primase lays down RNA primers so DNA polymerase can begin.
whyNot.3: RNA polymerase carries out transcription, not replication.

explain.body: In the nucleus, RNA polymerase reads the template strand to build mRNA (A to U, T to A, G to C, C to G). Pre-mRNA is processed: introns removed, exons spliced, 5' cap and poly-A tail added.

test.q: Which change happens when eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus?
options: Exons are removed; introns are spliced
Introns are removed; exons are spliced
A poly-A tail is added to the 5' end
test.why: Processing cuts out introns, splices exons together, and adds a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail.

whyNot.0: Reversed: introns are removed and exons are kept.
whyNot.1: RNA is built with uracil from the start; nothing is swapped during processing.
whyNot.3: The poly-A tail goes on the 3' end; the 5' end gets a cap.

explain.body: At the ribosome, each mRNA codon (3 bases) is matched by a tRNA anticodon carrying one amino acid; the ribosome forms peptide bonds. AUG starts (methionine); UAA, UAG and UGA stop. 64 codons, 20 amino acids.

test.q: How many different codons make up the genetic code?
test.why: There are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons: 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons.

whyNot.0: 20 is the number of amino acids, not codons.
whyNot.1: 61 is the number of codons that code for amino acids; the 3 stops bring the total to 64.
whyNot.2: 46 is the number of human chromosomes, not codons.

explain.body: Point mutations: silent (same amino acid), missense (new amino acid), nonsense (stop codon). Frameshifts (insert or delete, not a multiple of 3) change every later amino acid. The amino acid sequence (primary structure) sets how the protein folds, and shape sets function.

test.q: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain?
test.why: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, set directly by the mRNA codons.

whyNot.0: Secondary structure is local folding into alpha helices and beta pleated sheets.
whyNot.2: Tertiary structure is the overall 3-D shape from R-group interactions.
whyNot.3: Quaternary structure is two or more polypeptide chains joined, as in hemoglobin.
